title: Remote Ischaemic Conditioning for Fatigue After Stroke 2 (RICFAST 2)
summary:
Post-stroke fatigue is an overwhelming tiredness or lack of energy that does not get better with rest. It affects around half of people who have had a stroke. It can hold back recovery, make it harder to take part in everyday and social activities or to return to work, and reduce quality of life. There are currently no proven treatments for it.

Remote ischaemic conditioning (RIC) is a simple treatment that people can do at home using a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm. The cuff is inflated for 5 minutes and then let down for 5 minutes, and this is repeated 4 times, taking about 40 minutes in all. RIC briefly and safely reduces blood flow to the arm before letting it return. Research suggests this may help the body's cells produce energy more efficiently, improve blood flow and reduce inflammation. In our earlier small study (RICFAST), RIC done 3 times a week for 6 weeks was safe and well tolerated, and there were early signs that it might reduce fatigue.

This study (RICFAST 2) will find out:

* whether people with post-stroke fatigue can safely and comfortably do RIC at home more often (5 times a week) or for longer (12 weeks)
* whether enough people can be recruited to a study like this
* whether doing RIC more often or for longer might reduce fatigue more, and for longer, than the usual schedule or a comparison treatment
* how RIC might work in the body

Who can take part?

Adults who had a stroke between 3 months and 3 years ago and who have had troublesome fatigue for at least 6 weeks. People are being identified through stroke services, GP practices and community organisations in Sheffield, Doncaster, Rotherham and Barnsley (South Yorkshire, England).

What does the study involve?

60 people will take part. Each person will be put into one of four groups by chance (randomisation), with 15 people in each group. The groups differ in the pressure the cuff is inflated to (called "Pressure 1" and "Pressure 2"), and in how often and for how long the treatment is done:

* Group A (comparison group): cuff inflated to Pressure 1, 3 times a week for 6 weeks
* Group B: cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 3 times a week for 6 weeks
* Group C: cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 5 times a week for 6 weeks
* Group D: cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 3 times a week for 12 weeks

All the treatments cause a feeling of pressure in the upper arm. So that the results are fair, participants will not be told which cuff pressure is expected to have an effect.

Everyone will continue with their usual care. Participants will be shown how to use the cuff at home, can do the treatment at any time of day, and will keep a simple treatment log and symptom diary. The research team will phone or video call each week to check how things are going. Each participant will also wear a wrist activity tracker (Fitbit) throughout the study to record their steps, activity and sleep.

Questionnaires and tests of fatigue, mood, independence in daily activities, quality of life and walking will be done at the start of the study and 6 weeks, 12 weeks and 24 weeks (about 6 months) after starting treatment. The first three assessments take place at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, and the 24-week assessment can be done remotely. Travel expenses are paid.

Thirty participants from Groups A, B and C will be invited to have extra tests before treatment and after 6 weeks: an exercise test on a bike, a magnetic resonance (MRI) scan of the lower leg muscles to measure how much energy is stored in the muscle, and a blood test for markers of inflammation. Some participants will also be invited to an interview about their experience of doing the treatment at home.

What do investigators expect to find?

Investigators expect that people in all groups will be able to do the treatment at home, and that RIC done more often or for longer will lead to bigger and longer-lasting improvements in fatigue. The findings will be used to design a larger trial to test whether RIC is an effective treatment for post-stroke fatigue.
Background

Post-stroke fatigue (PSF) is a feeling of exhaustion that persists even after rest. It affects more than half of stroke survivors during their recovery, and around half of those affected report it as one of their worst symptoms. Stroke survivors and clinicians identify fatigue as a key limitation to post-acute rehabilitation. In the longer term, PSF impairs functional recovery, social engagement and return to work, and it is associated with reduced quality of life. Identifying effective treatments for PSF has been highlighted as a research priority for life after stroke both nationally and internationally, but no intervention has robust evidence of benefit.

The causes of PSF are multifactorial and include altered cortico-motor excitability, elevated inflammation and psychosocial factors. There is also mounting evidence implicating impaired mitochondrial function and cellular bioenergetics as a cause of fatigue in several clinical conditions. Impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism has been demonstrated in cancer-related fatigue, chronic fatigue syndrome, and neurological conditions with a very high prevalence of fatigue, including motor neurone disease and Parkinson's disease. Reduced muscle mitochondrial enzyme content has been found in severely fatigued older adults compared with non-fatigued counterparts, and impaired aerobic energy metabolism has been shown in the mitochondria of people with PSF. Addressing mitochondrial function is therefore likely to be an important component of PSF management.

Remote ischaemic conditioning as a potential treatment for PSF

Remote ischaemic conditioning (RIC) delivers brief, reversible episodes of limb ischaemia and reperfusion by cyclically inflating and deflating a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm. RIC improves cerebral blood flow in preclinical models and in clinical studies of vascular cognitive impairment and stroke, which is potentially relevant to the altered cortico-motor excitability seen in PSF. The release of vasoactive substances such as nitric oxide and adenosine in response to RIC improves endothelial reactivity and skeletal muscle perfusion in healthy people, which may mitigate the impaired sustained muscle contraction seen in post-stroke muscle fatigue. RIC may also moderate the inflammatory component of PSF by reducing inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6.

Most importantly, animal studies indicate several cellular pathways through which RIC may preserve mitochondrial oxidative capacity. RIC preserves mitochondrial respiratory chain function in the brain in mice and slows ATP depletion in porcine skeletal muscle after experimental ischaemic stress. In 22 chronic stroke survivors, two weeks of ischaemic conditioning significantly increased the duration of submaximal isometric paretic knee extension compared with sham, and our group has shown that RIC can increase walking speed and distance in people with multiple sclerosis. More than 48 clinical trials of ischaemic conditioning in stroke and cerebrovascular disease have not raised concerns about serious adverse events. These multimodal effects, particularly on cellular bioenergetics, make RIC a compelling therapeutic candidate for PSF.

Preliminary data: the RICFAST pilot trial

Investigators recently completed a pilot randomised controlled trial of the safety and tolerability of RIC for PSF (RICFAST; NCT03794947). Twenty-four participants with debilitating PSF were randomised to RIC (n=12) or sham cuff inflation (n=12), delivered as 4 cycles, 3 times per week for 6 weeks. Half of the participants self-delivered the intervention at home because of the COVID-19 pandemic. RIC was safe and well tolerated, with excellent adherence (91% of sessions completed).

Although the pilot was not powered to detect differences in fatigue, fatigue scores were lower in the RIC group than in the sham group at 6 weeks (adjusted between-group mean difference in FSS-7 -0.7, 95% CI -2.0 to 0.6), and the difference persisted at 6 months (-0.9, 95% CI -2.0 to 0.2). These differences are of similar magnitude to the clinically important difference for the Fatigue Severity Scale reported across clinical populations, including stroke (0.5 to 1.2). Between-group differences in 6-minute walk distance (+43.8 m, 95% CI -6.0 to 93.6) and in ventilatory anaerobic threshold favoured RIC, potentially indicating an increased capacity for aerobic adenosine triphosphate (ATP) metabolism. Phosphorus-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS) of tibialis anterior in 8 participants (4 RIC, 4 sham) showed increased resting ATP in all RIC participants, whereas resting ATP fell in sham participants.

It is not yet known whether more frequent or longer courses of RIC can be self-delivered at home by people with PSF, or whether they produce greater or more sustained benefit. RICFAST 2 addresses these questions and explores mechanisms of action.

Research question

Are more intense and longer RIC interventions feasible for people with PSF, and do they appear to be promising treatments for PSF?

Aim, objectives and hypotheses

The aim is to investigate the safety, tolerability and feasibility of differing treatment schedules of RIC in PSF and to understand its mechanisms of action.

Primary objective

1. To determine whether RIC self-delivered at home is feasible at a frequency of 3 times weekly for 6 weeks, 5 times weekly for 6 weeks, or 3 times weekly for 12 weeks. Hypothesis: participants in all treatment groups will find self-delivery of the intervention at home feasible.

   Secondary objectives
2. To determine whether an increased dose of RIC (frequency or duration of therapy) results in greater and more sustained improvement in PSF. Hypothesis: participants who undergo more intense or longer RIC will experience greater improvements in fatigue severity than those in the control or regular RIC groups.
3. To determine whether any benefits of RIC on fatigue are sustained beyond the end of treatment. Hypothesis: beneficial effects will be sustained at 24 weeks from the start of treatment, particularly in the long (12-week) RIC group.
4. To determine whether the effects of RIC occur through alterations in tissue ATP metabolism and improved anaerobic endurance. Hypothesis: RIC will increase resting skeletal muscle ATP, measured by 31P-MRS, and ventilatory anaerobic threshold, measured by cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
5. To determine whether people with PSF have a predominant fatigue phenotype or symptom profile using fatigue screening tools. Hypothesis: people with PSF differ in symptom characteristics, with some experiencing predominantly physical, cognitive or psychosocial symptoms.
6. To understand how PSF affects markers of physical activity measured with smart wearable devices. Hypothesis: people with more severe fatigue have lower levels of physical activity (e.g., step count).

Trial design

RICFAST 2 is a phase 2, four-arm, parallel-group, randomised controlled feasibility trial with participant blinding to cuff pressure and blinded outcome assessment. Sixty participants will be randomised 1:1:1:1 to one of four groups (15 per group). The trial includes an embedded mechanistic sub-study (30 participants: 10 from each of Groups A, B and C) and a qualitative interview study. The sponsor is Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, and the trial is funded by the Stroke Association.

Setting and participant identification

Participants are recruited through Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, with referrals from across South Yorkshire (Sheffield, Doncaster, Rotherham and Barnsley). Several identification routes are used so that the recruited population is inclusive and diverse:

* Community stroke rehabilitation teams share study information with people reporting significant fatigue after stroke, including people who have finished rehabilitation or never received it.
* The trial is promoted through the Stroke Association, posters in community care settings (such as the Sheffield Assessment and Rehabilitation Centre), regional Integrated Stroke Delivery Networks, and local and social media. The research team also runs information sessions with community groups that serve under-represented populations.
* Secondary care stroke databases are searched for people who had a stroke within the last 3 years and have agreed to be contacted about research. Invitations are prioritised towards areas with higher deprivation and larger ethnic minority populations. They are sent in waves, and targets are adjusted according to the characteristics of the people recruited so far.
* GP practices acting as participant identification centres search their records and send invitation text messages or emails, with a single reminder after 4 weeks.

People who do not respond to an invitation are contacted at least once more, so that those who find it difficult to initiate contact are not excluded.

Screening and consent

Interested people have a telephone or video screening call. The call includes a fatigue assessment and a clear explanation of the number of visits and assessments involved, to reduce missed visits and missing data later in the trial. Everyone screened is recorded on an anonymised screening log to inform the CONSORT flow diagram.

Written informed consent is taken face to face at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals by the principal investigator or a delegated, trained member of the research team, after at least 24 hours to consider the information. For people with aphasia, Part A of the Consent Support Tool is used to assess comprehension. Those who understand at least two key written and spoken words in a sentence receive an accessible, aphasia-friendly information sheet and consent form, developed in line with Stroke Association accessible information guidelines. Audio versions of the information sheet are available for people with reading difficulties, and an independent witness can countersign the consent form if a participant cannot sign because of arm impairment.

Eligibility is confirmed after consent at the baseline visit, including a mean FSS-7 score of 4 or more, and people of childbearing potential have a pregnancy test. Where possible, consent, eligibility confirmation, baseline assessment and randomisation take place in a single visit; they can be split across visits if the participant becomes fatigued. Consent is reconfirmed verbally at each visit, and participants' GPs are informed of their participation.

Interventions

All participants are trained face to face, with access to video explainers, to self-deliver the intervention at home in addition to usual care. Each session consists of placing a manual blood pressure cuff (Accoson) around the upper arm, inflating it to the allocated pressure for 5 minutes and deflating it for 5 minutes, repeated for 4 cycles (approximately 40 minutes). Participants inflate the cuff to a sticker marked on the pressure gauge and can complete sessions at any time of day. The four groups are:

* Group A (control): cuff inflated to Pressure 1, 3 times per week for 6 weeks (18 sessions)
* Group B (regular RIC): cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 3 times per week for 6 weeks (18 sessions)
* Group C (intense RIC): cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 5 times per week for 6 weeks (30 sessions)
* Group D (long RIC): cuff inflated to Pressure 2, 3 times per week for 12 weeks (36 sessions)

The control procedure uses the same cuff, cycle timing, training and support as active RIC. A comparable control protocol has been shown to maintain participant blinding in a previous RIC trial.

Participants complete a weekly treatment log and symptom diary. These record the sessions completed, any symptoms related to the intervention (rated on a 5-point scale) and any other therapies received. This approach to home delivery and fidelity monitoring was piloted successfully in RICFAST. Research staff phone or video call every participant each week to review adverse events, solve problems with treatment, and encourage adherence and log completion; all groups receive equal attention. If a problem with the intervention is identified, an unscheduled visit is arranged, which may include retraining, and the reason and any action taken are recorded.

Participants remain free to undertake other therapies, such as stroke rehabilitation, exercise or psychological therapies. Participants or clinicians may stop the intervention at any time. The reason is recorded, the participant reverts to usual care, and follow-up continues unless the participant withdraws from the trial.

Randomisation

After eligibility and consent are confirmed and baseline assessments are complete, participants are block randomised (1:1:1:1) by an independent researcher using an online system (Sealed Envelope Ltd). Randomisation is stratified by baseline modified Rankin Scale score (0-2 vs 3-4) and baseline FSS-7 score. Participants in the mechanistic sub-study complete their baseline cardiopulmonary exercise test and MRI scan before randomisation and the start of treatment.

Blinding

Participants are told that they will receive one of four treatment allocations, but not which one. All procedures produce a sensation of pressure in the upper arm, and participants are not told which cuff pressure is expected to be therapeutically active. Participants cannot be blinded to the frequency or duration of their treatment.

Follow-up assessments are carried out by a researcher blinded to treatment allocation, and 31P-MRS data are processed by a researcher blinded to group. Staff who train participants and make the weekly calls are aware of allocation. At the final follow-up visit, participants are asked which group they believe they were in, to assess the success of blinding.

Unblinding may take place if needed for participant safety or to assess the causality of serious or unexpected adverse events. Participants are offered unblinding at the end of the trial, once data entry and cleaning are complete and the final analysis plan has been signed off. Participants in the control group will not be offered active RIC after the trial, because its therapeutic benefit has not been established.

Assessments and follow-up

Follow-up time points are measured from the start of treatment, with a window of plus or minus 1 week:

* Baseline (face to face): sociodemographic and clinical data, medical history and examination, and measures of fatigue (FSS-7, MFIS), disability and independence (modified Rankin Scale, Barthel Index), mood (GAD-7, PHQ-9), stroke-specific and generic quality of life (Stroke Impact Scale, EQ-5D) and walking endurance (6-minute walk test). The activity tracker is also set up.
* Weekly during treatment (telephone or video, or face to face if needed): adverse events, adherence and troubleshooting.
* 6 weeks (face to face): end of treatment for Groups A-C. Baseline measures are repeated, adverse events and treatment logs are reviewed, and activity data are downloaded.
* 12 weeks (face to face): end of treatment for Group D. Baseline measures are repeated, adverse events and treatment logs are reviewed, and activity data are downloaded.
* 24 weeks (remote): questionnaire measures (no 6-minute walk test), adverse events, activity data download and participants' perceived allocation.

Assessments can be spread over more than one session to limit participant burden. Travel expenses of up to £20 per scheduled visit are reimbursed.

Wearable activity monitoring

Each participant receives a wrist-worn activity tracker (Fitbit Inspire 3) to wear throughout the 24 weeks of participation. People with hemiparesis wear it on the non-affected arm. Participants are asked to wear it as much as possible, including overnight, for at least 16 hours per day. Daily step count, sedentary time, distance moved, exercise time and total estimated sleep time per night are collected through a web API service, with project support from Google Health UK. To protect privacy, each device is linked to a generic research Google account that contains no personally identifiable information. Participants are advised that using the device means agreeing to the Google/Fitbit terms and conditions and privacy policy.

Mechanistic sub-study

Thirty participants (10 from each of Groups A, B and C) have additional assessments at baseline, before treatment starts, and at 6 weeks, the end of treatment for these groups.

Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) takes place at the Advanced Wellbeing Research Centre, Sheffield Hallam University, supervised by an exercise physiologist. Symptom-limited tests use an electronically braked upright cycle ergometer (Lode Corival) linked to MetaSoft Studio. Heart rate is monitored continuously (Polar H10) alongside blood pressure, and breath-by-breath respiratory data are collected through a Hans Rudolph face mask and a gas analyser (Cortex MetaLyzer 3B) calibrated before each test. Participants pedal unloaded for 3 minutes at a target cadence of 60 revolutions per minute. Work rate then increases by 10 W per minute until volitional exhaustion, symptom development (e.g., palpitations, faintness, pallor, confusion, loss of coordination or chest pain), or inability to maintain a cadence of 50 revolutions per minute. Outcomes are peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), ventilatory anaerobic threshold (VAT, estimated by the V-slope method), the minute ventilation/carbon dioxide output (VE/VCO2) slope and the oxygen uptake efficiency slope.

31P-MRS takes place at the Academic Department of Radiology, University of Sheffield, at 3 Tesla using a 31P/1H dual-tuned coil (Rapid Biomedical). Resting spectra are acquired with a pulse-acquire sequence from the proximal ankle dorsiflexors of both legs, including tibialis anterior. Coil placement around the tibial tuberosity is cross-checked for each participant to ensure consistency. A researcher blinded to group processes the spectra. Phasing and the frequency shift of phosphocreatine to 0 ppm are checked visually, 12 resonances are fitted using the AMARES algorithm in jMRUI, and the resulting amplitudes are corrected for T1 relaxation and normalised to total phosphorus signal. A full MR safety screen is completed at the scan visit.

Serum and plasma samples are collected at baseline and 6 weeks, processed and stored at the Clinical Research Facility, Royal Hallamshire Hospital, and analysed together at University of Sheffield laboratories once the final sample has been collected. The samples are analysed for IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, TNF-α, heat shock protein and GLP-1.

Qualitative study

Semi-structured interviews with at least 12 participants explore their experiences of self-delivering the intervention at home and its acceptability, continuing until content saturation is reached. Interviews take place in a quiet, private room and are audio-recorded. Recordings are deleted once transcribed, and transcripts are anonymised. The transcripts are analysed thematically in five stages: familiarisation, keyword selection, coding, theme development, and conceptualisation of the themes in relation to the existing literature on stroke and RIC.

Safety

Adverse events (AEs), including device-related events, and serious adverse events (SAEs) are recorded from randomisation until the final follow-up. They are identified at weekly contacts and follow-up visits and can be reported by any member of the clinical or research team. All events are recorded in the case report form, and the principal investigator assesses seriousness and relatedness to the intervention. Additional detail on SAEs is recorded within one working day of identification.

Expected AEs related to the intervention are skin petechiae, headache, arm paraesthesia, arm numbness, arm discolouration, and new or increased upper limb pain. In the mechanistic sub-study, injury during MRI related to a pacemaker, medical implant or other metallic object (failure of MR safety screening) is listed as expected. Pregnancies are reported to the Chief Investigator and Sponsor within 24 hours. Participants who become pregnant stop the intervention but continue follow-up, and the outcome of the pregnancy is collected.

Withdrawal and loss to follow-up

Participants may stop the intervention and remain in follow-up, or withdraw consent for further data collection at any time without giving a reason. Data collected before withdrawal are retained and included in the analysis. Participants who miss the 12-week assessment are still approached at 24 weeks. A participant is defined as lost to follow-up only if the 24-week assessment is not completed after all attempts to make contact.

Sample size

Between 12 and 20 participants per arm are recommended to estimate feasibility parameters and the standard deviation of outcome measures for future sample size calculations. Fifteen participants per arm (60 in total) will therefore be recruited. The trial is not designed to detect between-group differences in clinical outcomes.

Statistical analysis

Intervention and trial feasibility outcomes will be analysed with descriptive statistics and assessed against the pre-specified criteria for safety, acceptability, compliance and recruitment rate. Exploratory between-group comparisons of secondary outcomes will use one-way analysis of covariance of change from baseline, adjusted for age, baseline score and baseline modified Rankin Scale score (≤2 vs \>2), following the intention-to-treat principle. Adjusted mean differences with 95% confidence intervals will be reported for each time point.

Differences by fatigue type (predominantly physical, cognitive or psychosocial) will be explored using fractional polynomial models with an interaction term between treatment group and fatigue type. Associations between fatigue levels and physical activity data from the wearable devices will be examined with Pearson correlations. In the mechanistic sub-study, exploratory mediation analysis will examine whether changes in inflammatory markers mediate effects on fatigue.

Trial oversight and data management

The Chief Investigators have overall responsibility for the trial and supervise and review the data collected and the analyses performed. A trial management group meets approximately every 2 months, and at least monthly before key milestones. The funder has approved the membership of the oversight committees. All members of the research team have Good Clinical Practice training.

Data are recorded on paper case report forms identified only by a unique study number and are entered into an encrypted database on a password-protected Sheffield Teaching Hospitals research laptop. An enrolment log linking study numbers to identifiable information is kept separately, and study files are stored in a locked office at the Royal Hallamshire Hospital.

Patient and public involvement, equality, diversity and inclusion

The Sheffield Stroke Advisory Group has worked with the research team from the conception of the RICFAST pilot. The group helped develop this trial, including its design, recruitment predictions, outcome measures and use of wearable technology, and a lay representative is a co-investigator. On the group's advice, trial information will be available as explainer videos in the three most prevalent local languages (English, Punjabi and Urdu) and as easy-access materials for people with aphasia. The Consent Support Tool is used to tailor communication support to each participant throughout trial procedures.

The team works with Darnall Wellbeing, a community health organisation in an area of Sheffield with high ethnic diversity and socio-economic deprivation. Geographically targeted invitations are used to improve recruitment from under-served groups disproportionately affected by stroke, including people from Black and South Asian communities and people with lower socio-economic status. Participant engagement is supported by the HRA-endorsed Staying Connected toolkit. Lay members are supported in trial meetings through briefings, debriefings and a buddy system.

Dissemination

Results will be published in peer-reviewed journals, presented at clinical and academic conferences and submitted to the funder in a final report that will be made available online. Results will also be published on a freely accessible database within one year of trial completion, and progress summaries will be posted on the University of Sheffield website.

title: Testing VIRTUES Patient Care Sets in Cardiac Patients (VIRTUES Cardiac Care)
conditions: Heart Diseases Arrhythmias, Cardiac Atrial Fibrillation Cardiovascular Diseases Pathologic Processes
summary:
Patients with various cardiac conditions (such as those who experience a heart attack) are increasing in Canada and are in need of appropriate cardiac rehabilitation and care. Many patients do not have access to local in-person cardiac clinics, particularly in rural regions of Canada. A user-friendly digital application with accessible educational resources and recommendations based on the most up to date clinical practice guidelines can help mitigate these issues. VIRTUES is a digital healthcare application that targets 11 modifiable modules as follows:

1. antithrombotic management
2. lipid management
3. rate and rhythm control for atrial fibrillation
4. heart failure care
5. post myocardial infarction care
6. blood sugar management
7. blood pressure management
8. physical activity
9. healthy eating
10. smoking cessation
11. alcohol reduction

Of the 11 total modules, the first 7 listed provide recommendations in VIRTUES. The remaining 4 (physical activity, healthy eating, smoking cessation and alcohol reduction) consist of simple referrals to existing recommendations (i.e., for healthy eating and physical exercise) and referrals to existing local programs (i.e., for smoking cessation and alcohol reduction). Thus, in this cohort study, the investigators will test the primary 7 modules with 200 patients per module for approximately one month each in order to obtain feedback on the usability of each module. The investigators will also conduct virtual focus group discussions to obtain open ended feedback on the application. This study will provide valuable feedback, which will be used to improve and adapt the VIRTUES platform.
Heart conditions are on the rise in Canada, contributing substantially to patient quality of life. For example, over 60,000 Canadians will experience a heart attack per year. Other conditions, such as Atrial Fibrillation (in which the heart beats rapidly and irregularly) are also highly prevalent, with an estimated 250% increase by 2050. Unfortunately, few patients receive appropriate cardiac rehabilitation, and local in-person cardiac clinics are often inaccessible in rural regions. Patients need user-friendly, accessible educational resources based on current clinical practice guidelines. A digital interphase where patients can access their health information easily, and receive accurate medical advice can significantly help them manage their conditions. VIRTUES ("Virtual Integrated Reliable Transformative User Driven E-Health System") is a digital healthcare platform developed in partnership with the Cardiovascular Network of Canada (CANet). VIRTUES is a web application that uses built-in algorithms specific to each patient to make guideline-directed recommendations to patients and their healthcare providers and provide individually tailored educational material. VIRTUES includes the following 11 targeted modules:

1. antithrombotic management
2. lipid management
3. rate and rhythm control for atrial fibrillation
4. heart failure care
5. post myocardial infarction care
6. blood sugar management
7. blood pressure management
8. physical activity
9. healthy eating
10. smoking cessation
11. alcohol reduction

Of the 11 total modules, the first 7 listed provide recommendations to patients in VIRTUES. The remaining 4 (physical activity, healthy eating, smoking cessation and alcohol reduction) consist of simple referrals to existing local programs. The current cohort study tests the feasibility, usability, and patient experience of using VIRTUES in 200 patients across the 7 targeted modules that provide individually tailored recommendations. Each patient will only be exposed to module(s) specific to her/his condition. Testing will take place over the duration of approximately one month per module with approximately 1,400 patients in total (200 patients enrolled in each of the 7 modules). Patients will complete a series of forms assessing their medical history at the beginning of the study and they will be given a survey on their experience using VIRTUES after 6 and 12 months of using it. Patients will also be given an opportunity to volunteer for a virtual focus group discussion with other patients. The goal of this study is to provide insights on how to modify and improve VIRTUES based on patient feedback.

title: Effectiveness of Digital Cardiac Rehabilitation on Functional Capacity in Patients With Myocardial Infarction
summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if a digital health-supported cardiac rehabilitation program works to improve functional capacity, adherence, quality of life, and psychological status in cardiac patients. It will also learn about the effect of digital health support when added to conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does a digital health-supported cardiac rehabilitation program improve functional capacity?

How does digital health support affect patients' adherence to cardiac rehabilitation?

How does the program affect patients' quality of life and psychological status?

Researchers will compare digital health-supported cardiac rehabilitation combined with conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation to conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation alone to determine whether digital support improves functional, behavioral, and psychological outcomes in phase II cardiac patients.

Participants will:

Be randomly assigned to receive either digital health-supported hybrid cardiac rehabilitation in addition to conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation or conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation alone.

Have their functional exercise capacity assessed using the Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) as the primary outcome measure.

Complete assessments to evaluate cardiac rehabilitation adherence and engagement, health-related quality of life, and psychological status.

Have resting heart rate and blood pressure monitored as part of the clinical assessment.

Participants in the digital health-supported group will also use digital health tools for activity monitoring, exercise adherence, reminders, education, communication, and weekly telecoaching.
The Challenge:

Limited Participation in Cardiac Rehabilitation Cardiac rehabilitation is an important part of recovery and secondary prevention for patients with cardiovascular disease. However, participation in conventional center-based cardiac rehabilitation remains limited because of several barriers, including transportation difficulties, cost, work and family commitments, limited referral, and limited availability of rehabilitation programs. These barriers can be particularly challenging for patients living in underserved or low-resource settings, where participation and completion of rehabilitation programs may be poor.

The Goal of the Study :

This study aims to discover if a digital health-supported cardiac rehabilitation program can help improve functional capacity, adherence, quality of life, and psychological status in cardiac patients. Specifically, the research will evaluate the effect of adding digital health support to conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation compared with conventional cardiac rehabilitation alone.

How the Study Works? The study will involve 60 medically stable cardiac patients, both men and women, aged 55-65 years, who are eligible for Phase II outpatient cardiac rehabilitation following myocardial infarction and primary percutaneous coronary intervention.

These participants will be randomly divided into two equal groups:

The Digital Health-Supported Group: Participants will receive digital health-supported hybrid cardiac rehabilitation in addition to conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation for 12 weeks, with three sessions per week. They will use digital tools to support exercise adherence, activity monitoring, education, reminders, communication, and weekly telecoaching.

The Control Group: Participants will receive conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation alone for 12 weeks, with three sessions per week. They will also receive brief weekly phone contact without digital coaching.

Both groups will continue their prescribed medications and usual medical follow-up.

What is Being Measured?

To accurately determine whether the digital health-supported program is effective, the study will evaluate several key areas:

Functional Capacity: The Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) will be used as the primary outcome measure to assess functional exercise capacity by measuring the distance participants can walk in six minutes under standardized conditions.

Adherence and Engagement:

The study will assess adherence to the prescribed cardiac rehabilitation sessions. For participants receiving digital support, additional indicators such as platform use, completion of educational modules, and logged home-based activity will also be monitored.

Quality of Life:

Health-related quality of life will be evaluated using the MacNew Heart Disease Health-Related Quality of Life Questionnaire, which assesses physical, emotional, and social functioning.

Psychological Status:

Psychological status will be assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) to evaluate symptoms of anxiety and depression.

Physiological Measures:

Resting heart rate and blood pressure will also be assessed as part of the clinical evaluation.

Why This Matters Because participation in conventional cardiac rehabilitation can be affected by geographical, financial, and logistical barriers, finding accessible ways to support patients beyond the rehabilitation center is important. Digital health technologies such as smartphone applications, wearable monitoring, remote communication, and telecoaching may help patients remain engaged with their rehabilitation program.

By comparing digital health-supported cardiac rehabilitation with conventional outpatient cardiac rehabilitation alone, this study hopes to determine whether digital support can provide additional benefits in functional capacity, adherence, quality of life, and psychological status among Phase II cardiac patients.

* Clearance from a cardiologist to participate in the prescribed exercise program.

* A recent major cardiac event or intervention that has not yet been medically stabilized.
* Severe orthopedic, neurological, or pulmonary conditions that limit exercise testing or training.
* Severe cognitive impairment or communication difficulties that prevent adequate cooperation.
* Severe visual or hearing impairment that prevents safe use of the required digital technologies.
* Inability or unwillingness to use the digital rehabilitation platform, even with caregiver assistance.

title: Telerehabilitation for Post-Stroke Hand Function
summary:
This pilot randomized controlled trial will evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of a home-based, technology-enabled hand telerehabilitation program for adults with chronic stroke. Participants will receive either remotely guided hand training or a standard home exercise program matched for duration and intensity. Outcomes will include measures of hand function, adherence, and feasibility to assess the potential of telerehabilitation for improving access to structured post-stroke hand rehabilitation.
Persistent hand impairment after stroke is common and can substantially limit independence in daily activities. Access to intensive, task-specific hand therapy is often constrained by travel, cost, and availability of rehabilitation services, leading many individuals to rely on unsupervised home exercise programs. Telerehabilitation supported by low-cost technology may improve access to structured hand training while allowing remote supervision, but its feasibility and implementation in the home setting require systematic evaluation. This study aims to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of a hand telerehabilitation program for individuals with chronic stroke. The study will be conducted as a single-center pilot randomized controlled trial comparing two home-based interventions: (i) telerehabilitation and (ii) a standard home-advice exercise program matched for duration and intensity. Participants randomized to the telerehabilitation group will complete supervised home training sessions using technology-assisted activities to target hand function, delivered remotely via video conferencing. Participants in the control group will follow a home exercise plan similar to that used in typical post-stroke therapy. Outcome measures will be collected before and after the intervention and will include standardized assessments of hand function, as well as measures of adherence and feasibility. This study (i) involves adult stroke survivors, (ii) presents minimal risk, (iii) does not involve deception, (iv) does not collect sensitive health information, and (v) includes brief, noninvasive, and nonpainful interactions consistent with standard rehabilitation activities.

title: Multimodal Telerehabilitation of Rural Patients With Advanced Prostate Cancer
summary:
Prostate cancer has a significant impact on patient quality of life (QoL) directly, as well as through the management of localized disease (such as surgery and radiation-related incontinence, erectile dysfunction, and bowel dysfunction), and via direct side effects of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) resulting in a considerable physical and psychological burden. Recent studies demonstrated the efficacy of multimodal rehabilitation for functional recovery, improvements in QoL, reduction in cancer symptoms, and secondary and tertiary prevention. Despite the mounting evidence regarding the benefits of multimodal rehabilitation for this population, multiple barriers limit the access of prostate cancer survivors to cancer rehabilitation, especially in rural areas.

This study is a pilot study to assess usability, acceptability, and exercise adherence in 12-week multimodal telerehabilitation in patients receiving ADT with either high-risk or metastatic prostate cancer residing in rural areas.
Prostate cancer has a significant impact on patient quality of life (QoL) directly, as well as through the management of localized disease (such as surgery and radiation-related incontinence, erectile dysfunction, and bowel dysfunction), and via direct side effects of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) resulting in a considerable physical and psychological burden. Recent studies demonstrated the efficacy of multimodal rehabilitation for functional recovery, improvements in QoL, reduction in cancer symptoms, and secondary and tertiary prevention. Despite the mounting evidence regarding the benefits of multimodal rehabilitation for this population, multiple barriers limit the access of prostate cancer survivors to cancer rehabilitation, especially in rural areas.

Telemedicine approaches have the potential to improve access to cancer rehabilitation. This research team's previous studies showed a high acceptance of home-based telerehabilitation in older adults with chronic health conditions and a positive impact on QoL. In recent pilot usability studies, we demonstrated that multimodal telerehabilitation is well-accepted by patients with advanced bladder cancer who expressed strong interest in home-based cancer telerehabilitation. However, the feasibility of multimodal telerehabilitation in patients with advanced prostate cancer residing in rural areas has not been studied systematically. Additionally, barriers and facilitators of implementing prostate cancer telerehabilitation in rural areas are not well understood and require further exploration.

This study is a pilot study to assess usability, acceptability, and exercise adherence in 12-week multimodal telerehabilitation in patients receiving ADT with either high-risk or metastatic prostate cancer residing in rural areas.

The enrolled patients will have access to a tailored cancer rehabilitation program via a home-based telerehabilitation system, remote supervision, and interactive education and counseling sessions to enhance support and adherence. A comprehensive assessment by a physical therapist will be conducted remotely using the previously validated app. After the initial assessment, the patients will be individually prescribed resistance and aerobic exercises based on metastasis location, pain, fatigue, and current fitness levels. Physical exercises specific to prostate cancer, such as pelvic floor exercises, will be tailored to individual impairments. Interactive education on exercise benefits and safety, behavioral change strategies, principles of lifestyle changes, and vocational, cognitive, and sexual rehabilitation will be provided via the telerehabilitation system. Social support will be delivered via group tele-counseling sessions. Automated analysis of daily exercise logs will alert the telerehabilitation team about low exercise adherence and prompt tailored feedback to the patients. As in this research team's previous interventions, support will be available throughout the study to assist patients in using the telerehabilitation system successfully.

title: Remote Rehabilitation in Patients With HFpEF (PATRON-HF)
conditions: Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction
summary:
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by typical symptoms of heart failure, structural and functional cardiac abnormalities, and elevated serum levels of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), despite preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. Typical symptoms of HFpEF include reduced exercise tolerance, exertional dyspnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and orthopnea.

It is estimated that approximately 35 million people worldwide suffer from HFpEF, including approximately 3 million patients in the United States. The exact number of patients with HFpEF remains unknown; however, the prevalence of the disease is increasing. Risk factors for HFpEF include obesity, arterial hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and advanced age. Patients with HFpEF are hospitalized an average of 1.4 times per year, and the annual mortality rate is approximately 15%. To date, the most effective approach to the management of HFpEF has been the control of comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension, coronary artery disease, and obesity.

Remote rehabilitation (RR) has already become an established component of modern cardiology. It is widely used in developed countries, and its popularity continues to increase. Its main advantages include reduced costs for both patients and healthcare payers compared with traditional, center-based rehabilitation. In addition, for patients living far from rehabilitation centers or those with limited access to transportation, remote rehabilitation provides a solution to improve access to care.

The efficacy and safety of remote rehabilitation have been demonstrated in cardiac patients with coronary artery disease and in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). However, to date, the safety and efficacy of remote rehabilitation in patients with HFpEF have not been sufficiently investigated. Therefore, the aim of the proposed study is to assess the safety and efficacy of remote rehabilitation in patients with HFpEF.
Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF) is an increasing challenge. HFpEF is primarily associated with significant limitations in exercise tolerance due to feelings of breathlessness and shortness of breath. As the disease progresses, the severity of symptoms deepens, preventing normal functioning and significantly limiting daily activities-such as shopping, cleaning, walking, or socializing. These symptoms are associated with a significant decline in quality of life. Moreover, HFpEF is characterized by the need for recurring hospitalizations and frequent outpatient visits to specialists, which significantly burdens the healthcare system. Patients suffering from HFpEF also have a significantly increased risk of death compared to the healthy population. Pharmacotherapy for HFpEF offers limited benefits; so far, only one drug has been proven to limit symptoms somewhat and reduce the risk of hospitalization, but it does not impact mortality; these are inhibitors of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2. A more effective treatment form for this patient group is cardiac rehabilitation. However, this involves very large financial outlays and is often impossible for logistical reasons. Moreover, rehabilitation cannot be conducted all the time. A solution to this problem could be home rehabilitation, which is much cheaper and more accessible, and the patient can use it for a long time. Given the above, the study aims to assess the safety and effectiveness of home rehabilitation in patients with HFpEF. The study is designed as a randomized, blinded, multicenter trial in which 110 patients diagnosed with HFpEF will be included. Each arm will include 55 patients diagnosed with HFpEF based on the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) definition of 2021. Each patient qualifying for the study will have a stress test on a cycle ergospirometer, a panel of laboratory tests including both a basic panel and the concentration of selected adipokines and inflammatory markers in serum blood and the quality of life will be assessed. Additionally, coronary microcirculation will be performed. Based on the stress test on the cycle ergometer, the training load for the time of home rehabilitation will be determined. Then, a bicycle ergometer and a set of sensors for telerehabilitation will be delivered to the patient's home, and the study participant will be trained in its use. Then, for 12 weeks, the study group will have four weekly home rehabilitation sessions with remote care.

The control group of 55 patients will be treated according to standard therapy. After 12 weeks, all participants will again undergo the stress test on the ergospirometer, an analogous set of initial laboratory tests, and an assessment of quality of life. Patients will again have performed an assessment of coronary microcirculation. An independent team will assess any adverse event to ensure the safety of home rehabilitation.

The endpoints in the proposed study will be the evaluation of physical performance parameters obtained during ergospirometry, left ventricle filling parameters, and the quality of life of patients. Appropriately conducted home rehabilitation can significantly improve the performance of patients with HFpEF assessed in the stress test; moreover, parameters of left ventricle filling will also improve. Improving these parameters has a proven impact on reducing the risk of death, frequency of hospitalizations, and quality of life of patients with HFpEF.

title: Evaluation of a Remote Behavioural Stress Recovery Intervention for Myocardial Infarction Patients Younger Than Fifty-five (BRIM-55): A Feasibility Study
conditions: Cardiac Disease Depression and Quality of Life Cardiac Distress Myocardial Infarction Psychological Distress Anxiety
summary:
The goal of this feasibility study is to learn if the randomised controlled trial evaluating the Remote-delivery Balance in Everyday Life (rBEL) programme for adults younger than 55 years who have experienced a myocardial infarction (MI), is feasible.

The objective is to examine the feasibility of the rBEL programme and the associated study procedures before a controlled evaluation of the programme. This is an uncontrolled, single-arm, pre-post treatment designed study.

Participants of the target population will take part of the six session over 13 week programme. Feasibility will be evaluated against predefined feasibility criteria regarding study procedures and programme acceptability.
BACKGROUND Even though there have been major improvements in medical treatments resulting in considerably lower mortality rates, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of death and the main cause of loss of disability-adjusted life-years worldwide. Myocardial infarction (MI) is the most common of the serious CVDs. While the total number of MIs has decreased during the last decades, the proportion of young patients hospitalized with MI has increased.

Cardiac distress (CD) summaries the psychological impacts of a cardiac event and expands on the general "psychological distress" concept (i.e. symptoms of depression and anxiety). Cardiac distress is common after an MI. For young persons, having an MI is particularly stressful and the prevalence of anxiety and depression is more than double compared to that of older patients.

Conventional stress management intervention programs are based on a "reactivity paradigm", with techniques used to reduce, avoid, or change the interpretation of the stressors and/or stress responses associated with distress. An alternative, contrasting strategy is to address recovery processes. To the best of our knowledge, the intervention program Balance in Everyday Life (BEL), based on cognitive behavioural principles, has the best empirical support.

Guidelines for cardiac rehabilitation recommend screening of psychosocial aspects but interventions in this area are very rare in clinical practice.

METHOD Aim The aims are to assess feasibility and acceptability of the iBEL program for post-myocardial infarction survivors aged below 55 years reported ongoing CD, and the study procedures of the later evaluation study.

Research Questions

1. How feasible is the study procedures of the planned evaluation study in terms of recruitment, retention and adherence rates?
2. To what extent is the iBEL program perceived as acceptable to young post-MI survivors, in terms of its content, delivery method and relevancy?

Design An uncontrolled, single-arm, pre-post treatment design.

Participants Thirty participants of the target population will be included. Exclusion criteria: (i) not being able to read, write or speak Swedish, (ii) being able to use the digital device necessary for participation and (iii) early retirement or disability pension at the time of the MI.

Procedure Participants will be recruited via a register extraction from SWEDEHEART of all persons having an MI before the age of 55 one year before intervention start. Preliminary eligible participants will be sent an invitation letter primarily via a digital post-box with a description of the study and an option to register interest for the study. To qualify as participants with CD, they must state they have at least experienced moderate distress as a consequence of their MI which impairs day-to-day recovery, and they believe psychological support will benefit them. They are then asked to provide written consent.

The Program The program consists of 6 sessions spread out over 13 weeks. Each session includes a video-call meeting online, via the platform Zoom, with a therapist. The therapists are healthcare workers (clinical social workers-LCSW, MSW specialized in psychotherapy, nurses psychiatric/mental health nurse practitioners- PMHNPs, occupational therapists with mental health specialization) with training in clinical conversations or students recruited from the final semesters of the university programs for psychologists or physiotherapists with basic training in clinical conversations. They will be trained in the rBEL program and receive supervision by a senior therapist. Before each data collection time-point, participants will be prompted and, if necessary, reminded to report via SMS and/or e-mail, based on their preference, and thereafter, if needed, via telephone.

In addition to this meeting with the therapist there is psychoeducational material on a website (www.brim55.se) and a printed booklet for exercise notations.

Data analysis The feasibility results will be evaluated against pre-specified progression criteria. The sample size (N=30) is based on a rule-of-thumb for feasibility studies and is judged to be enough for detecting feasibility concerns.

* Insufficient Swedish proficiency for study procedures,

title: Exercise Support and Rehabilitation for Patients After Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection
summary:
The study aims to examine the feasibility of a remote exercise program in women recovering from spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) events (heart attacks). Heart attacks caused by SCAD are different to the traditional heart attacks. In SCAD a tear happens within the blood vessels causing partial or full blockage. The population affected by SCAD is hugely different to the population affected by other 'traditional' heart attacks; as SCAD mainly happens in otherwise healthy women. From historical cases, SCAD has been associated with strenuous exercise, however, medical research did not find a link. The recovery after SCAD is also very different from other 'traditional' heart attacks. Cardiac rehab programmes are designed for an older population therefore they may not be suitable for a younger predominantly female population. This study will examine if a remote-exercise programme is achievable in people after a SCAD event.
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a rare condition that leads to myocardial infraction (MI). Young women make up 87-95% of SCAD events, which is also the leading cause of MIs occurring after pregnancy. Following any MI event, cardiovascular rehabilitation (CR) is recommended, which includes supervised exercise sessions, and interventions to reduce risk factors, improve psychosocial wellbeing, and increase medication adherence. Evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) show that CR reduces cardiac events and decreases mortality but this evidence is largely generated in a population with atherosclerotic disease. Trials of CR include mostly male participants, typically aged in their mid-sixties therefore CR guidelines may not be appropriate for the SCAD population who significantly differ in pathophysiology, age and gender compared with the population for which CR has been developed and tested.

Previous observational data suggested an association with strenuous exercise and SCAD, however, no casual link has been established. Clinical advice on exercise following SCAD is conflicting due to the lack of RCTs and therefore evidence. Consequently, many SCAD patients experience psychological distress, fear, and anxiety about exercise, avoiding all exercise which may lead to predictable long-term health consequences. Well-tested recovery programmes in SCAD are required to offer informed and tested exercise-based support to reduce the fear and hesitancy that may lead to exercise avoidance. This is particularly needed for women, who constitute the majority of SCAD diagnoses but are less likely to be referred to, attend, or adhere to CR. Small studies have explored the feasibility of SCAD survivors' participation in CR , however, programmes in these studies used conservative guidance preventing participants to reach pre-morbid exercise levels. This is problematic as (a) if participants are asked to exercise at levels well below their functional capacity, a rehabilitation effect is unlikely (b) such advice potentially reinforces that only lower levels of exercise are safe. This highlights the challenges SCAD survivors have in knowing what is safe and effective in terms of exercise. Therefore, this project aims to improve what we know about exercise and physical activity after SCAD.

The investigators will aim to test if women who have survived a SCAD will take part in a two-arm feasibility randomised controlled study of a 12-week remote exercise programme, what levels of exercise duration and intensity they achieve, and what they think about it. The two-arm design (usual care + blinded wearable activity monitor \[control\] and exercise intervention, + cardiopulmonary exercise test(CPET), + wearable activity monitor \[intervention\]) has been chosen to allow for the use of CPET at baseline to ensure safe exercise prescription.

title: Telerehabilitation Exercise Program for Postoperative Recovery in Lung Cancer.
summary:
Lung cancer is one of the leading causes of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide. Thoracic surgery remains the treatment of choice for patients with early-stage disease; however, postoperative recovery is frequently associated with reduced functional capacity, decreased physical activity levels, pulmonary complications, dyspnea, and impaired quality of life. Early physiotherapy interventions are recommended to minimize these adverse outcomes, although access to postoperative rehabilitation services remains limited in many healthcare settings, including the Andalusian Public Health System.

Telerehabilitation has emerged as a promising strategy to improve access to rehabilitation services by delivering therapeutic exercise and clinical follow-up remotely. Previous studies have demonstrated that telerehabilitation is safe, effective, and cost-efficient across different clinical populations. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness in patients recovering from lung cancer surgery remains limited.

This single-blind randomized controlled trial aims to compare the effects of an eight-week telerehabilitation program based on therapeutic exercise with usual postoperative care in patients with lung cancer undergoing thoracic surgery. Participants allocated to the intervention group will receive 24 therapeutic exercise sessions and 8 online clinical follow-up sessions delivered through the Rehbody platform over an 8-week period. Outcomes will include functional capacity, dyspnea, physical activity level, postoperative pulmonary complications, and health-related quality of life.

The study is designed to address the following research question: In adults with lung cancer undergoing thoracic surgery (Population), does an eight-week therapeutic exercise-based telerehabilitation program (Intervention), compared with usual postoperative care (Comparison), improve postoperative recovery as measured by functional capacity, dyspnea, physical activity level, postoperative pulmonary complications, and quality of life (Outcomes)?
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide and continues to impose a substantial burden on healthcare systems. Surgical resection is considered the standard treatment for patients with resectable disease and offers the best opportunity for long-term survival. However, despite advances in surgical techniques and perioperative care, recovery following thoracic surgery is frequently characterized by impaired physical function, reduced exercise capacity, dyspnea, decreased physical activity levels, postoperative pulmonary complications, and deterioration in health-related quality of life.

The physical and functional consequences of lung cancer treatment may persist for months or years after surgery and can negatively affect independence, participation in daily activities, and overall well-being. Postoperative rehabilitation and therapeutic exercise have therefore become important components of comprehensive cancer care. Early physiotherapy interventions aim to prevent postoperative pulmonary complications, facilitate recovery of physical function, reduce symptom burden, and promote a safe return to daily activities. Previous studies have shown that exercise-based rehabilitation following lung resection can improve functional capacity and quality of life while reducing postoperative morbidity.

Despite these recognized benefits, access to structured rehabilitation programs remains limited in many healthcare settings due to geographical, logistical, organizational, and resource-related barriers. This challenge is particularly relevant in publicly funded healthcare systems, where rehabilitation services may not be universally available after hospital discharge. As a result, many patients do not receive adequate follow-up rehabilitation during a critical phase of postoperative recovery.

Telerehabilitation has emerged as a promising alternative model of healthcare delivery that enables rehabilitation services to be provided remotely through digital technologies. This approach has the potential to improve accessibility, continuity of care, adherence to prescribed exercise programs, and patient engagement while reducing travel requirements and healthcare costs. Growing evidence supports the safety, feasibility, and effectiveness of telemedicine and telerehabilitation interventions across a variety of chronic and oncological conditions.

In patients with lung cancer, recent studies have reported encouraging results regarding the use of mobile applications and remotely supervised rehabilitation programs. These interventions have been associated with improved adherence to treatment, enhanced functional recovery, better pulmonary function, increased physical activity levels, reduced symptom burden, and improvements in quality of life. Furthermore, digital rehabilitation strategies may facilitate long-term monitoring and support during the postoperative period, helping patients maintain active participation in their recovery process.

Nevertheless, important knowledge gaps remain. The number of high-quality randomized controlled trials specifically evaluating structured postoperative telerehabilitation programs after lung cancer surgery is still limited. Existing studies have often included small sample sizes, heterogeneous interventions, or mixed cancer populations, making it difficult to establish definitive recommendations regarding the optimal design and clinical effectiveness of telerehabilitation in this population. Additional research is needed to determine whether remotely delivered therapeutic exercise programs can produce clinically meaningful improvements in postoperative recovery and patient-centered outcomes.

The present randomized controlled trial has been designed to address this evidence gap by evaluating the effectiveness of an eight-week telerehabilitation program based on therapeutic exercise in patients undergoing thoracic surgery for lung cancer. Participants allocated to the intervention group will receive a structured and progressive exercise program delivered through a dedicated telerehabilitation platform, combined with regular online clinical follow-up sessions. The intervention incorporates aerobic exercise, muscle strengthening exercises, respiratory muscle training, individualized progression, and continuous monitoring of adherence and symptoms. Participants assigned to the control group will receive the usual postoperative physiotherapy care routinely provided after thoracic surgery.

The study will evaluate the impact of the intervention on key dimensions of postoperative recovery, including functional capacity, dyspnea, physical activity levels, postoperative pulmonary complications, and health-related quality of life. Assessments will be performed before surgery, after completion of the intervention period, and following a short-term follow-up period to explore the maintenance of potential benefits.

The findings of this study may contribute to the development of evidence-based rehabilitation pathways for patients recovering from lung cancer surgery. If effective, this telerehabilitation model could represent an accessible, scalable, and cost-efficient strategy for improving postoperative outcomes and expanding access to rehabilitation services within routine clinical practice.

title: Home-based Cardiac Rehabilitation in Heart Failure
summary:
This study evaluates a mobile health (mHealth) home-based cardiac rehabilitation program for patients with heart failure. We will stratify randomization between rural and urban populations, with the goal to assess implementation of cardiac rehabilitation across these two geographic areas. . The study will randomize 332 patients with heart failure (ejection fraction ≥35%) who are not eligible for center-based rehabilitation to either a 12-week mHealth cardiac rehabilitation program or an attention control group, with outcomes measured over 6 months using a composite endpoint of mortality, hospitalizations, and quality of life. We will then assess the implementation of the intervention.
Background and Significance:

Rural communities in the United States experience a disproportionate burden of cardiovascular disease and associated adverse outcomes, with recent epidemiological data demonstrating a widening mortality gap compared to urban populations. These disparities are particularly pronounced in cardiovascular care delivery, where rural-residing adults demonstrate significantly lower rates of guideline-directed therapies for coronary heart disease, heart failure, and stroke. Among the most substantial gaps identified is the utilization of cardiac rehabilitation services, with total participation among Medicare beneficiaries reaching only 5% in rural areas. This disparity is compounded by the intersection of multiple risk factors including reduced access to healthcare services, lower socioeconomic status, and geographic barriers to specialized care.

The emergence of telemedicine platforms presents a novel opportunity to address these healthcare access disparities through innovative service delivery models. The COVID-19 pandemic has catalyzed the adoption of digital health technologies, with telemedicine visits among rural Medicare beneficiaries increasing nearly 100-fold between 2019 and 2020. Concurrent improvements in rural broadband access, with over 70% of rural adults reporting home broadband availability in 2021, have created an infrastructure foundation supporting telehealth interventions. Mobile health (mHealth) interventions have demonstrated efficacy in cardiovascular care through patient monitoring, medication adherence support, and risk factor management, with preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness in reducing rehospitalizations and increasing patient participation in cardiac rehabilitation programs.

Study Design and Methodology:

This investigation employs a randomized, open-label, Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial design to evaluate the efficacy and implementation characteristics of an mHealth-enabled home-based cardiac rehabilitation program. The study will enroll 332 adult participants with recent hospitalization for heart failure with ejection fraction ≥35%, stratified with 70% recruitment from rural hospitals and 30% from urban centers to enable comparative analysis of implementation challenges across geographic settings. Participants will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either the mHealth cardiac rehabilitation intervention or attention control, with outcomes assessed over a 6-month follow-up period.

Intervention Components:

Participants randomized to the mHealth cardiac rehabilitation group receive a comprehensive remote monitoring kit delivered via overnight shipping, containing a wireless blood pressure monitor, resistance bands, and a wearable monitor. These hardware components integrate with the Movn Health platform, which participants access through a smartphone application offering both synchronous and asynchronous features including real-time video consultations with exercise coaches, exercise videos for self-directed sessions, one-to-one messaging capabilities, and automatic data synchronization from all monitoring devices.

The 12-week cardiac rehabilitation program implements a multi-domain physical rehabilitation approach. The intervention begins with a comprehensive assessment evaluating exercise capacity and safety requirements. Each participant follows a personalized exercise regimen.

Participants in the attention control group receive a FitBit device for activity monitoring and step count tracking, along with bi-weekly telephone calls throughout the 12-week intervention period to minimize contact differential between study arms. These telephone interactions focus on general health discussions without providing specific exercise counseling or rehabilitation guidance.

Outcome Measures and Assessment:

The primary endpoint employs a composite hierarchical outcome structure analyzed using a win-ratio methodology, incorporating all-cause mortality, time to first heart failure hospitalization, total heart failure hospitalizations, and a 5-point difference in quality of life assessed by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire. This analytical approach provides a comprehensive evaluation of intervention effectiveness across multiple clinically relevant domains while accounting for the relative importance of mortality and morbidity outcomes.

Secondary endpoints include individual components of the primary composite outcome, physical activity levels measured through FitBit-recorded daily step counts, and general health-related quality of life assessed using the EuroQol 5 Dimension 5 Level instrument. Additional secondary measures encompass mental health parameters evaluated through the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 scale, and the Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly.

The study incorporates comprehensive implementation outcome assessment using the RE-AIM framework, evaluating Reach through the number of eligible participants receiving the intervention, Effectiveness through perceived relative advantage and observed outcomes, Adoption through adherence rates and contextual factors, Implementation through fidelity measures and cost analysis, and Maintenance through persistence and discontinuation rates. A sequential mixed-methods approach will conduct semi-structured interviews with 12 clinicians across all sites and 36 patients across study arms to evaluate acceptability, preferences, and contextual factors influencing implementation effectiveness.

title: TeleheartCR vs. Clinic-Based Cardiac Rehabilitation After Acute Coronary Syndrome
summary:
Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is an effective evidence-based intervention that improves outcomes in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), but many eligible patients do not complete the program. A hybrid CR intervention that combines telehealth, home-based, and clinic-based components (TeleheartCR) may increase participation by addressing barriers to access while maintaining the functional capacity benefits of traditional CR. The purpose of this study is to conduct a randomized controlled trial comparing TeleheartCR with traditional clinic-based CR in patients with ACS to evaluate differences in program adherence and pre-to-post program change in functional capacity.
Over 1 million patients are hospitalized annually in the United States for an acute coronary syndrome (ACS; myocardial infarction or unstable angina). Accordingly, CR is recognized as a Class I, Level A recommendation for secondary prevention in ACS survivors. Yet less than a quarter of eligible cardiac patients utilize CR in the US. Even among patients who initiate CR, fewer attend all prescribed CR sessions, with lower rates observed among those with low socioeconomic status (SES), and racial and ethnic minoritized groups. Low and disparate CR adherence harms patients, as evidence suggests a dose-response relationship, such that each additional CR session attended reduces morbidity and mortality. Innovative program designs are needed to deliver sustained, equitable CR participation among ACS patients.

The central hypothesis of this research study is that TeleheartCR will show greater program implementation (better adherence \[primary\], acceptability, and appropriateness) and will be just as effective (non-inferior pre- to post-intervention change in functional capacity \[primary\], health-related quality of life, and cardiorespiratory fitness) relative to clinic-based CR. The TeleheartCR program includes up to 36 sessions delivered through a combination of clinic-based and home-based sessions and is typically completed over approximately 12 weeks. To allow for scheduling flexibility and clinical considerations, participants may be allowed up to 6 months post-enrollment to complete the program and outcome assessments. To formally test the hypothesis, the investigator will conduct an adequately powered effectiveness-implementation hybrid type I randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing the TeleheartCR program vs. clinic-based CR among ACS patients.

Specifically, this study will determine the degree to which the TeleheartCR program improves CR adherence, clinical outcomes (e.g., functional capacity), and equitable cost/access (i.e., across SES, racial, and ethnic groups) relative to clinic-based CR among ACS patients.
